initial_posts.narrative: As a retired patient in North Carolina, I've seen how new regulations often start with good intentions but limited resources. For the No Surprises Act in 2022, I expect the federal enforcement budget to be around $50 million—enough to set up complaint systems and some audits, but not enough to handle the huge volume of complaints from millions of patients. The number of certified IDR entities will be small, maybe 15, because the certification process is new and complex, and they'll be concentrated in big cities, leaving rural areas like parts of my state underserved. Many plans, especially smaller ones, won't have their systems ready to calculate the Qualifying Payment Amount accurately—I'd guess only about 60% are fully prepared, because building data systems takes time and money that many plans didn't invest before the law passed.
evidence: Federal enforcement budgets for new health laws typically start modestly; $50 million is plausible for initial staffing, IT systems, and outreach, but insufficient for full complaint processing and audits across all states.

The IDR entity certification process is new and rigorous; only a handful of organizations will be ready by early 2022, likely fewer than 20, and they will cluster in urban areas, limiting geographic coverage.

Many group health plans, especially self-insured ones, lack the data infrastructure to calculate median contracted rates accurately; industry surveys suggest only about half to two-thirds of plans will be QPA-ready by the start of 2022.

initial_posts.narrative: From my perspective as a nonparticipating anesthesiologist in California, the federal enforcement budget for 2022 will be around $40 million. This is less than what patient advocates might hope for because the administration is still ramping up and has competing priorities. The complaint volume will be high, but enforcement will be reactive rather than proactive, with limited capacity for audits or corrective actions. Certified IDR entities will number about 12, as the certification process is slow and many potential entities are hesitant due to low case volumes and uncertain revenue. Geographic distribution will be uneven, with most entities in major metropolitan areas, leaving rural regions underserved. Only about 55% of plans will have fully operational QPA systems at the start of 2022. Smaller and self-insured plans often lack the data infrastructure to calculate median contracted rates accurately, and many are still negotiating data access agreements. This will lead to frequent disputes over QPA accuracy, which I will have to navigate in IDR cases.

Geographic distribution will be uneven, with most entities in urban areas, leaving rural regions underserved. Only about 55% of plans will have fully operational QPA systems at the start of 2022. Smaller and self-insured plans lack the data infrastructure to calculate median contracted rates accurately, and many are still negotiating data access agreements. This aligns with Sarah Chen's and Maria Gonzalez's estimates, and I disagree with Curry Citizen's higher 60% because our internal surveys showed slower readiness among smaller plans.
